Jonas/Claire —

AEs are already getting asked (a lot) for a “replication guide” for the latency/$ numbers. Can you send:

1) A short SE talk track (2–3 mins) for calls: what they *can* do to reproduce, what will differ, and the caveats.
2) A PoC checklist we can share 1:1 with prospects under NDA (or at least something we can paraphrase).

Common questions we’re hearing:
- “If we run the same prompts, will we get your numbers?”
- “Is caching/batching on? Are you measuring streaming?”
- “How much does region/network affect it?”
- “What’s the minimum setup to validate the claim quickly?”

If helpful, I can consolidate into an internal one-pager for Sales/SE.

Thanks,
Markus

Yep. Here’s a first pass you can use immediately. Claire will add detail on the harness / manifests.

SE TALK TRACK (2–3 minutes)

What to say:
- “The report is reproducible in the sense that the harness, prompt mix, and run configuration are fixed and versioned. If you run the same inputs under similar concurrency in the same region, you should see results within a tight band.”
- “The numbers are not magic single-run screenshots — we repeat runs, apply stability gates, and publish variance notes. You should expect some drift if any of: region, time-of-day capacity, output token length, or your network path differs.”
- “We’re optimizing for production economics, so we measure end-to-end request latency and cost; not just raw tokens/sec. That’s why the core metric is latency per dollar, and we show p50/p95 alongside.”

What NOT to say / avoid (for legal + credibility):
- Don’t claim “you will get exactly these numbers” or “always faster than X.”
- Don’t imply the metric is a universal proxy for all workloads; always anchor to “workload definitions” (context length + output length + concurrency + streaming mode).
- Don’t compare competitor pricing/latency unless the prospect provides their own measured baseline; our public report should stay “directional” where competitors are mentioned.

Quick answers to the common questions:
- Caching/batching: We run with the benchmark’s defined policies (documented). Continuous batching is part of the serving runtime; we don’t turn off the runtime’s scheduling. We do *not* rely on “cheating” via prompt-specific caches. Prefix/KV reuse across identical prompts is disabled for the public runs (unless explicitly stated). (See methodology section for the exact setting.)
- Streaming: Public metric is based on end-to-end request timing (TTFT + decode). We also track TTFT internally; if a prospect’s app is streaming-first, we can guide them to validate TTFT separately.
- Region/network: Region matters materially. For replication we recommend running the client from the same cloud region/zone (or a VM close to it) to reduce WAN noise.

Recommended “minimum PoC” steps (fast validation)
- Pick 10–20 representative prompts from their product (or use our v3 production mix prompts if they won’t share).
- Pin: model version, region, max output tokens, temperature/top_p.
- Run at 3 concurrency points that match their expected peak (e.g., 1 / 8 / 32) and capture p50/p95.
- Compare latency and cost on Redwood Hosted vs their current baseline using the same token limits.

If you need a single sentence:
- “You can reproduce the results by running the versioned harness with the same prompt mix and concurrency in the same region; expect small variance from network and capacity, and treat cross-provider comparisons as directional unless measured under the same conditions.”

Claire will send a shareable checklist + the exact settings language.

Jonas

—
Jonas Weber
Director, Performance & Evals | Redwood Inference

Adding the “how to reproduce” details. This is written to be safe to share under NDA (or paraphrase publicly without the repo specifics).

REPRODUCIBILITY NOTES (what we mean, concretely)

A run is reproducible when these are held constant:
- Harness version (commit SHA / release tag)
- Prompt set version (v3 production mix)
- Workload definition:
  - input token distribution (prefill)
  - output token distribution (decode)
  - concurrency schedule
  - streaming mode (on/off)
- Region + model deployment target (same region, same model revision)
- Sampling parameters + max output tokens

What we do internally (so prospects understand “not cherry-picked”):
- Warmup phase (discarded)
- Multiple repetitions per (model, region, workload)
- Stability gate: auto-rerun if p95 variance exceeds threshold
- We keep raw logs + run manifests for audit

What will still vary even if they do everything right:
- Their client location (WAN adds jitter; especially on TTFT)
- Time-of-day or temporary regional fleet constraints
- Output length drift if prompts aren’t identical or if they allow unbounded completion length

Recommended prospect replication pattern (lowest friction)
1) Client location: spin up a small VM in the same cloud region as the target endpoint and run tests from there.
2) Pin everything: region, model version, and token limits.
3) Use fixed seeds where applicable (or do N repeats and average) to reduce token-length randomness.
4) Capture p50, p95, and throughput; do not over-index on a single p95 outlier.

If they want to align exactly with the report:
- We can share the run manifest schema and a sample manifest (NDA). The manifests specify: prompt set ID, concurrency schedule, token limits, streaming, and measurement windows.

Methodology references for SE (internal)
- Confluence: “Latency per $ benchmark methodology”
  https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/display/AML/Latency+per+$+Benchmark+Methodology
- Runbook (region sweeps):
  https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/display/ENG/Benchmark+Report+Runbook+-+Region+Sweeps

Suggested “safe” caveat line for customer-facing emails
- “Benchmark results are workload-dependent and may vary based on prompt mix, output length, region, and client network path. We can help you reproduce the methodology for your workload and validate the economics in a PoC.”

If you want, I can put this into a 1-page PDF for the enablement kit.

Claire

—
Claire Dubois
Sr Research Engineer (Evals/Benchmarks) | Redwood Inference

This is great.

Two follow-ups so we don’t get ourselves in trouble on calls:

1) Can we explicitly say “prefix caching across identical prompts is disabled” or is that too implementation-specific / might change? I want to avoid an AE saying “caching is off” and being wrong.
2) For “latency/$”, prospects ask “is that just (latency) / (price)?” Do we have a one-liner definition that’s accurate but simple?

If you can send those two lines, I’ll draft the internal one-pager + email template.

Markus



From: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: SE talk track: how prospects can reproduce benchmark results (and what not to claim)

On (1): I’d avoid absolutes like “caching is off.” Safer language:

- “We don’t rely on prompt-specific caching to inflate results. The methodology documents what’s enabled (e.g., the serving scheduler/continuous batching) and what’s not enabled (e.g., reuse across repeated identical prompts unless explicitly stated).”

That stays true even if we adjust implementation details later.

On (2): Simple definition we’ve been using internally:

- “Latency per dollar is the observed end-to-end latency for a defined workload, normalized by the model’s per-token cost for that same workload. It’s a way to compare ‘speed at a given spend’ rather than speed alone.”

If they press for math, you can say:
- “We compute cost from counted input+output tokens using published pricing for the run; then we normalize latency by that cost so you can compare cost-adjusted performance.”

(We can provide the exact formula in the methodology appendix; I’d keep it out of live calls unless they ask.)

Jonas

One more nuance worth including for SE:
- If a prospect’s baseline provider truncates/streams differently, token counts may not match. Ask them to cap max output tokens and compare on a fixed token budget.

Also, for prospects who want to replicate on their own infrastructure: we should steer them to Redwood Dedicated/Private evaluation plans rather than implying the hosted report numbers will match 1:1 on arbitrary hardware.

Claire
